overview:
Sarvārthasiddhi (also spelled Sarvarthasiddhi) is a classical Jain Sanskrit commentary on Ācārya Umāsvāmī’s Tattvārthasūtra, traditionally dated to around the 5th–6th century CE and attributed to the Digambara monk Ācārya Pūjyapāda (also known as Devānandi). It is regarded as the oldest extant, and one of the most authoritative, line‑by‑line expositions of the Tattvārthasūtra, a foundational Jain scripture that systematically presents Jain ontology, cosmology, ethics, and the path to liberation in aphoristic form.

The title “Sarvārthasiddhi” literally means “accomplishment of all meanings” or “realization of all purposes,” indicating the commentator’s aim to unfold the full import of each sūtra. The work belongs to the Digambara exegetical tradition but has been widely studied across Jain sects, including Śvetāmbara and Sthānakavāsī communities, because Tattvārthasūtra itself is accepted as a pan‑sectarian doctrinal text. Sarvārthasiddhi thus occupies a central place in Jain philosophical education as a bridge between terse aphorisms and systematic doctrine.

Structurally, Sarvārthasiddhi follows the ten‑chapter organization of Tattvārthasūtra. Each chapter begins with the relevant sūtras and then offers a word‑by‑word gloss, grammatical clarification, and doctrinal explanation. The ten thematic divisions are: (1) Right Faith and Right Knowledge, (2) The Category of the Living (jīva), (3) The Lower and Middle Worlds, (4) Celestial Beings, (5) The Category of the Non‑Living (ajīva), (6) Influx of Karma (āsrava), (7) The Five Vows and ethical discipline, (8) Bondage of Karma (bandha), (9) Stoppage and Shedding of Karma (saṃvara and nirjarā), and (10) Liberation (mokṣa). Through these chapters, Sarvārthasiddhi expounds the seven fundamental categories (tattva) recognized in Jainism—jīva, ajīva, āsrava, bandha, saṃvara, nirjarā, and mokṣa—and integrates them into a coherent path of spiritual practice.

Philosophically, Sarvārthasiddhi is notable for articulating the Jain doctrine of non‑absolutism (anekāntavāda) and the related theory of standpoints (naya) and conditional predication (syādvāda), even when these terms are not always foregrounded explicitly. By carefully distinguishing different modes, attributes, and relations of substances, Pūjyapāda shows how permanence and change, identity and difference, and unity and plurality can be reconciled without collapsing into one‑sided metaphysical claims. The commentary emphasizes that reality is multi‑faceted and that valid knowledge must respect the complexity of substances and their states.

In the ethical and soteriological sections, Sarvārthasiddhi elaborates the three jewels (ratnatraya) of Jainism—Right Faith (samyag‑darśana), Right Knowledge (samyag‑jñāna), and Right Conduct (samyag‑cāritra)—as inseparable components of the path to liberation (mokṣa‑mārga). It classifies knowledge into sensory (mati), scriptural (śruta), clairvoyant (avadhi), telepathic (manaḥparyāya), and omniscient (kevala), and distinguishes indirect (parokṣa) from direct (pratyakṣa) cognition. The text also analyzes the vows (vrata), restraints, and disciplines required of householders and ascetics, linking ethical conduct to the processes of karmic influx, bondage, stoppage, and shedding.

Cosmologically, Sarvārthasiddhi provides detailed descriptions of the Jain universe (loka), including the lower, middle, and upper worlds, the various classes of celestial beings, and the spatial and functional roles of non‑living substances such as dharma (medium of motion), adharma (medium of rest), ākāśa (space), pudgala (matter), and kāla (time). These expositions are not merely descriptive; they serve to situate the soul’s journey within a vast, beginningless cosmos governed by karmic law.

Historically, Sarvārthasiddhi has inspired multiple modern translations and critical editions. Professor S. A. Jain’s English translation, published under the title “Reality” by Jwalamalini Trust (1992), is widely cited for its clarity and fidelity to the original. More recently, Vijay K. Jain has produced an edition of Tattvārthasūtra with English explanation drawn from Sarvārthasiddhi, further consolidating the commentary’s role in contemporary Jain studies. Scholarly assessments emphasize Sarvārthasiddhi’s literary elegance, philosophical depth, and its enduring capacity to address perennial questions about the nature of reality, knowledge, and liberation.

While Sarvārthasiddhi is deeply respected, it is still a commentary—its authority is rooted in its close reading of Tattvārthasūtra and the broader Jain tradition, rather than in any claim to supersede primary scripture. Modern students are encouraged to read it alongside the sūtras themselves, other traditional commentaries, and qualified teachers, especially when applying its teachings to contemporary ethical and practical dilemmas.

primary_sources.title: Sarvārthasiddhi (commentary on Tattvārthasūtra)
primary_sources.author: Ācārya Pūjyapāda (Devānandi), Digambara tradition
primary_sources.original_text:
तत्त्वार्थसूत्राणि
सर्वार्थसिद्धिः

(Example opening invocation from Tattvārthasūtra, which Sarvārthasiddhi comments upon)
सम्यग्दर्शनज्ञानचारित्राणि मोक्षमार्गः ॥ १.१ ॥
primary_sources.translation: “The path to liberation consists of Right Faith, Right Knowledge, and Right Conduct.” (Tattvārthasūtra 1.1, as explained in Sarvārthasiddhi)
primary_sources.notes:
Sarvārthasiddhi is a Sanskrit vṛtti (commentary) on the Tattvārthasūtra, traditionally attributed to Ācārya Pūjyapāda, a Digambara monk renowned as a poet, grammarian, philosopher, and scholar of Ayurveda. It is considered the oldest extant commentary on Tattvārthasūtra and is structured into ten chapters corresponding to the ten chapters of the sūtra text: (1) Faith and Knowledge, (2) The Category of the Living, (3) The Lower and Middle Worlds, (4) The Celestial Beings, (5) The Category of the Non‑Living, (6) Influx of Karma, (7) The Five Vows, (8) Bondage of Karma, (9) Stoppage and Shedding of Karma, and (10) Liberation.

In each section, Sarvārthasiddhi provides a word‑by‑word gloss of the sūtras, clarifies grammatical constructions, and offers doctrinal explanations grounded in Jain metaphysics and ethics. For example, on Tattvārthasūtra 1.1, the commentary explains that Right Faith is the non‑deluded apprehension of reality, Right Knowledge is accurate cognition of substances and their modes, and Right Conduct is behavior aligned with non‑violence and other vows, all three being mutually supportive aspects of the path to mokṣa.

The text survives in multiple manuscript traditions and has been critically edited and translated in modern times. Notable modern resources include S. A. Jain’s English translation “Reality” (Jwalamalini Trust, 1992), which presents Sarvārthasiddhi in English with extensive notes, and Vijay K. Jain’s edition of Tattvārthasūtra with English explanation based on Sarvārthasiddhi (Vikalp Printers, 2018). These works help situate Sarvārthasiddhi within both traditional Jain pedagogy and contemporary academic study.

primary_sources.title: Tattvārthasūtra (Mokṣaśāstra)
primary_sources.author: Ācārya Umāsvāmī (Umāsvāti), accepted by both Digambara and Śvetāmbara traditions
primary_sources.original_text:
तत्त्वार्थसूत्रम्

जीवाजिवाः पुण्यपापाः आस्रवो बन्धः संवरः निर्जरा मोक्षः ॥
(Representative sūtra summarizing the seven categories, as discussed extensively in Sarvārthasiddhi)
primary_sources.transliteration:
tattvārthasūtram

jīvājivāḥ puṇya‑pāpāḥ āsravo bandhaḥ saṃvaraḥ nirjarā mokṣaḥ ||
primary_sources.translation: “The soul and the non‑soul, merit and demerit, influx, bondage, stoppage, shedding, and liberation (are the fundamental categories).”
primary_sources.notes:
Although Tattvārthasūtra is itself a primary text rather than Sarvārthasiddhi, it is inseparable from the commentary’s function and must be considered alongside it. Sarvārthasiddhi systematically unpacks sūtras such as this one, explaining the nature of jīva (living substance), ajīva (non‑living substance), puṇya and pāpa (merit and demerit), āsrava (influx of karma), bandha (bondage), saṃvara (stoppage of karmic influx), nirjarā (shedding of karma), and mokṣa (liberation).

In the commentary, Pūjyapāda clarifies that these categories are not merely abstract; they describe the dynamic relationship between the soul and karmic matter. The soul, characterized by consciousness (upayoga), becomes bound by karmic particles through activities (yoga) actuated by passions (kaṣāya). By cultivating Right Faith, Right Knowledge, and Right Conduct, and by practicing vows and restraints, the aspirant gradually stops new karmic influx and sheds existing karmas, ultimately attaining the state of omniscience (kevala‑jñāna) and liberation.

Modern editions that present Tattvārthasūtra with Sarvārthasiddhi include the work of Vijay K. Jain, which offers the Sanskrit text, English translation, and explanatory notes based on the commentary. These resources are valuable for students seeking to understand how Sarvārthasiddhi reads and interprets the sūtras in detail.

misconceptions.myth: Sarvārthasiddhi is an independent scripture that replaces or supersedes the Tattvārthasūtra in authority.
misconceptions.reality: Sarvārthasiddhi is a commentary (vṛtti) on the Tattvārthasūtra, not a standalone scripture meant to replace it. Its authority derives from its close, tradition‑aware exposition of the sūtras and its alignment with broader Jain doctrine, but the primary text remains Tattvārthasūtra itself. Responsible study treats Sarvārthasiddhi as an interpretive guide to the sūtras, to be read alongside them and in conversation with other commentaries and qualified teachers.

misconceptions.myth: Sarvārthasiddhi belongs exclusively to one Jain sect and is not relevant outside the Digambara tradition.
misconceptions.reality: While Sarvārthasiddhi is authored by a Digambara monk and is a cornerstone of Digambara exegesis, Tattvārthasūtra—the text it comments on—is accepted by both major Jain sects. As a result, Sarvārthasiddhi has been studied and respected across sectarian lines, including by Śvetāmbara and Sthānakavāsī scholars. Sectarian differences in interpretation do exist, but they do not render the commentary irrelevant to other traditions; instead, they invite comparative study and careful attention to lineage‑specific readings.

misconceptions.myth: Sarvārthasiddhi presents a rigid, one‑sided metaphysical system that denies plurality of viewpoints.
misconceptions.reality: Far from being one‑sided, Sarvārthasiddhi exemplifies the Jain commitment to non‑absolutism (anekāntavāda). By distinguishing substances, modes, and standpoints, and by carefully analyzing how attributes relate to different conditions, the commentary shows how apparently conflicting views—such as permanence and change or identity and difference—can be reconciled without collapsing into dogmatic extremes. The text encourages nuanced, multi‑faceted understanding rather than rigid metaphysical claims.

misconceptions.myth: Reading Sarvārthasiddhi alone is sufficient for making complex modern ethical, medical, or legal decisions.
misconceptions.reality: Sarvārthasiddhi is a classical doctrinal commentary focused on metaphysics, cosmology, ethics, and the path to liberation in its traditional context. It does not directly address many contemporary issues in medicine, mental health, law, or finance. Applying its teachings to modern dilemmas requires careful interpretation, contextual knowledge, and often consultation with qualified human experts—such as learned Jain teachers, medical professionals, or legal advisors—rather than relying solely on the text or on secondary summaries.
